name: Yusuf Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew for Northline Grid, the company that runs the big high-voltage lines between the power stations and the towns. Most days we're forty or fifty metres up a steel tower, changing insulators or repairing a conductor, hanging off a harness. I'm crew lead, so I give the safety briefing at the base before anyone climbs, and I'm the one who signs the work permit.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being away. When a storm drops towers two regions over, we're gone ten days at a time, sleeping in motels. My partner Lina is in her second year of nursing school, so for now I'm the only pay coming in, and I'm on the lower tier of our contract because I was hired after 2019. Same tower, same height, eleven percent less than the man next to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. I'll read you five short pictures of the future and ask about each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I use one of those AI chat tools now and then, mostly to help me write emails for the union, so I'm not a complete stranger to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about what actually matters, like the two-tier contract. AI being a bit of hype doesn't surprise anyone who climbs towers for a living. Online I'd share a joke about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and nothing changing isn't great either. I'm still eleven percent behind the older crew, Lina still has two years of school, and we've got about three weeks of money saved. The real problem was never AI, it was the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep climbing and keep taking storm trips, because those pay double time. I'd help the union build the case to end the lower tier before the contract runs out in 2028, which means collecting pay slips from every crew. And we'd keep cooking at home instead of eating out, which Lina and I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit tired, like when you're halfway up a tower and realise you've still got the other half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Collecting pay slips from every crew sounds like a lot of work. How would you do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. I'd photograph them at the depot on Monday mornings and put the numbers in a spreadsheet, and I'd probably ask the AI tool to help me lay it out. That's about the most I'd use it for. A good table of real pay slips will win more than any speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at home would feel a tight month most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, honestly. I've sent her a bit every month since my dad passed, and that's the first thing I'd protect. Lina and I can eat lentils for a month; my mum shouldn't have to.

say: AI being **hype** surprises nobody who climbs towers for a living.
Let's talk about what matters instead, like the **two-tier contract**.
think: Nothing changing isn't great either; I'm still **eleven percent** behind the older crew.
The real problem was never AI, it was the **contract**.
do: Keep taking **storm trips** for the double-time pay.
Collect **pay slips** from every crew to build the case against the lower tier.
Keep **cooking at home** instead of eating out with my partner.
feel: **Steady** but tired, like being halfway up a tower with half still to climb.
S0.quote: A good table of real pay slips will win more than any speech.
fieldNote: His grievance is the **two-tier contract**, not technology, and he keeps returning to it.
He'd use AI only as a **spreadsheet helper** for union work.
The money he sends his **mother** is the first thing he would protect.

steps.text: Take every storm restoration trip offered this winter
Collect crew pay slips to fight the lower contract tier
Cook at home and skip eating out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit the office before it hits the towers, and we should look after the office people. Line design, outage planning and customer calls are all thinking work. The company owes those folks retraining, not a goodbye email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my crew is fine for a while, and that makes me feel a bit guilty. Drones already take most of our inspection photos, and in this picture software would sort them and send us straight to the bad insulator. That means less walking the line and more fixing, which honestly I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to read the drone and sensor reports properly, because whoever reads them well ends up leading the job. Once two or three other crews had used the new planning software, I'd ask for the training. And I'd bring a motion to the union to make the company pay for retraining for anyone in the office whose job shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for other people than for me. It's like watching the ground floor flood while you're on the top floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for two or three other crews first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen first versions of things nearly kill people. We had a new fall-arrest system once that looked great on paper and jammed in the cold. I'll go second or third every time, and I'll go willingly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change things at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, which is a relief. Lina's going into nursing, and from what you read out, nobody's replacing nurses with a chatbot. If anything, it feels like we picked the right two jobs by accident.

say: It will hit the **office** before it hits the towers.
The company owes office staff **retraining**, not a goodbye email.
think: My crew is fine for a while, and that makes me feel **guilty**.
Software sorting **drone photos** means less walking the line and more fixing.
do: Learn to read the **drone and sensor reports** properly to stay crew lead.
Ask for **planning software** training once two or three crews have used it.
Bring a **union motion** for company-paid retraining for office staff.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more for other people than for myself.
S1.quote: We had a new fall-arrest system once that looked great on paper and jammed in the cold.
fieldNote: He sees the change landing on **office colleagues** first and feels guilty about it.
He adopts tools **second or third**, pointing to a fall-arrest system that jammed in the cold.
His partner's **nursing** career makes the household feel safer in this picture.

steps.text: Learn to read drone and sensor inspection reports
Bring a union motion for paid retraining of office staff
Keep leading his tower crew as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a plan, fast, and the government should be writing it this week, not next year. I'd post the union's statement and share it everywhere. People who keep the lights on shouldn't be the last to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my climbing days end around 2031, and the crew lead part ends sooner, because planning and permits are exactly what the AI does first. By 2028 I'm just a pair of hands that a screen points at a tower. The good news is Lina finishes nursing school in 2028, so we'd have one solid wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the storm trips that aren't worth it and keep the ones that pay double. I'd put away every bit of overtime so we have three months saved by the time Lina qualifies. I'd ask the union which robot maintenance training is actually proven, and once there's one with real jobs at the end, I'd sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, though. More like the feeling before a big storm job, when you know it'll be bad but you know the drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lina about who earns what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Lina that she might end up carrying us for a while, and that I'm fine with that. My dad would have hated it, but I'm not my dad. Lina carried my lunch up the hill when I was an apprentice, so I can let her carry this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the work do you think a robot would struggle with longest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Storm work, in my opinion. A tower down in a muddy field at night, with wires wrapped round trees, is nothing like a tidy test site. But you said as well as people, so I'd rather plan for that than argue with it.

say: Workers need a **plan**, and the government should write it this week.
People who keep the lights on shouldn't be the **last to know**.
think: My **crew lead** role goes first, because planning and permits are AI work.
My climbing ends around **2031**, but my partner qualifies as a nurse in 2028.
do: Keep only the **double-pay** storm trips and drop the rest.
Save every bit of **overtime** to reach three months by 2028.
Sign up for **robot maintenance** training once a proven course exists.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, like before a big storm job when you know the drill.
S2.quote: By 2028 I'm just a pair of hands that a screen points at a tower.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking side** of his lead role going before the climbing does.
He'd accept his partner being the **main earner** and says he isn't his father.
Even under pressure he waits for a **proven** course before signing up.

steps.text: Save storm overtime until three months of costs are put aside
Rely on his partner's nursing wage from 2028
Enrol in robot maintenance training once one has real jobs attached

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this right if we start now. I'd want the union and the company sitting down in the first year to agree how many robots, how fast, and what happens to the crews. If it's planned, people can take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to watch who does well and copy them, which suits me. By 2031 the paperwork side of being crew lead is gone, and by 2034 the towers. I'd be thirty-five, which isn't old, but I'd need a new trade by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years watching the companies that try robots on towers and talking to the crews who work beside them. Around year three I'd pick a course, probably robot maintenance or substation commissioning, which means testing new equipment before it goes live. And I'd vote for whoever puts a real retraining fund into law, not just a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than the fast one. Five years is long enough to be careful, and being careful is how I do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about those robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my old apprentice Tomás, who moved to a big contractor in the city that loves new gear. If anyone's seen a tower robot up close, it's his crew. I'd buy Tomás a beer and ask what breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much more than now, since we already live small. Maybe the summer trip to see Lina's family. That one hurts, because it's the only real holiday we take.

say: **Five years** is enough to do this right if we start now.
The union and company should agree **how many robots**, and how fast, in year one.
think: I'd have time to **watch** who does well and copy them.
I'd need a **new trade** by thirty-five, when the towers go.
do: Talk to crews working beside **tower robots** for the first two years.
Pick a course in **robot maintenance** or substation commissioning around year three.
Vote for whoever puts a **retraining fund** into law.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier, because five years leaves room to be careful.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to be careful, and being careful is how I do everything.
fieldNote: Five years suits his **careful** style: watch first, then commit around year three.
He plans to learn from an **old apprentice** at a city contractor.
Cutting the yearly **family trip** is the sacrifice that hurts him most.

steps.text: Ask crews at the city contractor what their tower robots get wrong
Enrol in robot maintenance or commissioning training in year three
Vote for a retraining fund written into law
Skip the summer trip to his partner's family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Ten years is two contracts. If the union can't win a fair deal on robots in two contracts, that's on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd relax a bit. Lina would be a nurse with a few years behind her, I'd be in my late thirties, and the robots don't come till 2039. There's room to build savings and maybe even a family before any of it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep climbing for the first five years and try to get us to two months of savings. Around 2030 I'd start commissioning training at night, once the first graduates have jobs. Lina and I would probably get married in the next couple of years instead of waiting, because this picture gives us the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a quiet way. It'd be at the back of my head, not on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd marry sooner. Why does this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the other pictures made us want to wait and save. With ten years, waiting just means waiting. My mum keeps asking, and in this one I'd finally have an answer for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the AI arriving in 2036 worry you, before the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The permits and the switching orders, maybe. If the AI writes the switching orders and gets one wrong, a crew could touch a line they think is dead. I'd want a person still checking every switching order until the AI has a clean record.

say: **Ten years** is two contracts, so nobody has an excuse.
If the union can't win a **fair robot deal** in that time, that's on us.
think: I'd **relax** a bit, with the robots not coming until 2039.
There's room for **savings** and maybe a family before any of it lands.
do: Keep climbing and build **two months** of savings over five years.
Start **commissioning training** at night around 2030, once graduates have jobs.
Marry my partner in the **next couple of years** instead of waiting.
feel: **Uneasy** in a quiet way, at the back of my head, not on my chest.
S4.quote: If the AI writes the switching orders and gets one wrong, a crew could touch a line they think is dead.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his worry into **wedding plans**, not just savings.
His one live fear is an AI-written **switching order** that gets a line wrong.
He holds the **union** responsible for using the two contracts well.

steps.text: Build two months of savings from tower work
Start commissioning training at night around 2030
Marry his partner within the next two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Lina wouldn't be qualified yet, we'd have three weeks of savings, and the crew lead side of my job would go first. What would help is a retraining fund the companies pay into, with real jobs at the end, and help with rent for families while one person retrains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but nobody asks who's checking the switching orders. Getting that wrong is how lineworkers die, not how they lose their jobs.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but nobody asks who's checking the switching orders.
portrait: Yusuf Ziegler, 27, leads a **transmission tower crew** for a regional grid company.
He's the only earner while his partner trains as a **nurse**, with three weeks saved.
His long fight is the **two-tier contract** that pays him eleven percent less.
He adopts new tools **second or third**, never first, and plans carefully.
His mood runs from **uneasy** to anxious, easing as the warning time grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, before his partner qualifies and with only three weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** paid by the companies, with real jobs at the end.
Help with **rent** for families while one person retrains.
